transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because... I just can't shake this feeling that I failed. As a father, you know? And just... as a useful person in general. It keeps looping in my head, over and over, until I feel like I don't really deserve much of a future. 

It's funny, actually, thinking about the future. I used to have this whole plan when I was in grad school. I was going to write this book on, well, it doesn't matter now, but I had this professor, Dr. Aris... he always wore these terrible tweed jackets that smelled like old pipe tobacco. He told me I had a brilliant mind for research. I spent months in the library, just surrounded by stacks of books, drinking terrible coffee from that machine in the basement. You know the kind that tastes like burnt plastic? Anyway, I thought I was going to do something important. But now... I just sit around, and that loop just keeps playing. I don't even know where all those research notes ended up. Probably in a box in the garage, getting ruined by the damp. The garage roof has been leaking for years, and I just... I haven't fixed it. I should have fixed it.
Have you noticed that you don't enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you've lost interest in activities you once cared about?

Yeah... yeah, that's exactly it. I used to really look forward to things. Like, I have this model railway setup in the spare room. O scale, mostly. I spent three years just building the mountain landscape for it. I used this special plaster technique I learned from a guy at the hobby shop—Gary, I think his name was. He had this incredible setup in his basement, took up the whole room. He used to work for the railroad, actually, out in Colorado. Anyway, I used to love working on it. But now... the trains just sit there, half-built, collecting dust on the table. I walk past the room and I don't even want to turn the light on. 

And it's the same with the Cubs games. I used to watch them with my daughter all the time. We had this whole ritual, ordering pizza from that place down the street... the one that closed last year and turned into a dry cleaner. Why do we need so many dry cleaners? But now, even just turning the TV on to put a game on feels... pointless. I just don't care who wins anymore.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

Yeah, I guess so. Just... heavy, you know? Like there's a wet wool blanket over everything, from the minute I wake up. Which is usually pretty early, unfortunately. The garbage trucks come by our street at, like, 5:15 in the morning. It's ridiculous. They changed the route back in October, and ever since then, it's just this massive grinding noise before the sun's even up. I tried calling the city about it, but you know how that goes. You just sit on hold listening to that terrible smooth jazz music for twenty minutes before someone transfers you to a voicemail that's full. My neighbor, Tom, he actually went down to the municipal building to complain. Tom's a retired lawyer, so he loves arguing with people. He's got this pristine lawn, too. Spends hours out there with these little clippers... but anyway, yeah. Most of the day, every day, I just sit there feeling... empty. Like I'm just taking up space.

Has your mood been worse at a particular time of day, like in the morning, or have you noticed any changes in how you think or perceive things, such as hearing voices or having thoughts that others might not understand?

Worse at a particular time? I don't really think so. It's just... always there. Just a constant, flatline kind of heavy, no matter what the clock says. Though I guess mornings are when I'm standing in the kitchen trying to make coffee, and my old French press actually shattered in the sink the other day. I'd had that thing since I lived in Chicago, back when I was still trying to finish my dissertation. I went down to the local hardware store to see if they sold replacement glass carafes. The guy who runs it—Mike, I think, always wears this faded blue apron with a tear in the pocket—he told me they don't carry parts like that anymore. Said nobody fixes anything, they just buy a new one. Everything's just disposable now, isn't it? You buy something, it breaks in a year, and you just throw it in a landfill. It's a real shame how much waste we produce. 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, voices and things. No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear anyone talking to me or see things that aren't there. It's just my own thoughts, which are pretty miserable, but they're definitely just mine. Nothing unusual like that.
Have you noticed that you've been moving more slowly than usual, or that it takes you longer to get things done, even simple tasks like getting dressed or making a cup of tea?

Moving slowly? I... I don't really think so. I haven't noticed anything like that. I mean, it takes me a while to get out of bed, but once I'm up, I move around fine. I'm not moving through molasses or anything. Though, speaking of tea, I did try to make a cup of that Earl Grey yesterday. The loose leaf kind, not the bags. My sister sent it to me for my birthday last year. She lives up in Seattle now, works for this tech startup that makes... I don't even know, some kind of software for organizing digital receipts. She's always been the organized one. When we were kids, she used to color-code her entire closet. Shirts by sleeve length, then by color. It was exhausting just looking at it. She's been trying to get me to visit her out there, says the rain is actually really soothing. But flying right now is such a nightmare, isn't it? The lines at security, and they always make you take your shoes off, which I never understood why they still do that. I have this pair of loafers that are just impossible to get back on without a shoehorn. 

But no, I haven't noticed moving any slower than normal. Just... everything feels pointless, so I don't do much. But when I do, it's at a normal speed, I guess.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently, like eating a lot less or more than usual, or losing or gaining weight without trying?

Well, yeah, actually. I've definitely had to tighten my belt a notch or two over the last month. Most days I just don't even bother making a real meal. I'll just sit there and realize it's, like, 8:00 PM and I haven't eaten anything all day. And then I can only manage to choke down some toast or a bowl of cereal. I used to buy that cereal with the almonds in it, Honey Bunches of Oats, I think? But the last time I went to the grocery store, they had completely rearranged the aisles. I hate when they do that. You go in knowing exactly where the cereal is, aisle four, right next to the oatmeal, and suddenly it's the baking aisle. Flour everywhere. And the prices, don't even get me started. A box of cereal is like seven dollars now. Who can afford that? I saw this woman in front of me at the checkout, she had a cart full of name-brand stuff and she paid with a hundred dollar bill. You don't see those much anymore, do you? The cashier had to hold it up to the light and use one of those special markers to make sure it wasn't fake. My uncle used to work for the Treasury Department, actually. He told me all sorts of stories about counterfeit rings in the 80s... 

But yeah, anyway, I'm just not eating much. Just toast, mostly. I just forget, or I just don't care enough to make anything.
Have you noticed that you have less energy than usual, or that even small tasks feel exhausting to you?

Less energy? Oh, God, yes. I'm just completely drained. It really doesn't matter how long I've been in bed, either. I could lie there for twelve hours, and even simple things, like carrying the laundry upstairs or just sorting the mail, it feels like I'm moving through wet cement. 

Speaking of the mail, actually, our regular guy, Stan, he just retired last month. Walked this same route for twenty years. He always had those little milk bone treats in his pocket for the neighborhood dogs. Now we've got this new kid, can't be older than twenty-two, and he constantly puts my neighbor's magazines in my box. They get *Architectural Digest*. I used to flip through it back when I was thinking about remodeling the kitchen, back when I actually cared about doing things to the house. But the prices of lumber went so high a couple of years ago, remember that? A single sheet of plywood was like ninety bucks. Absolute insanity. My brother-in-law is a contractor down in Florida, and he said the supply chain issues were just completely ruining his business. He had to delay this massive beachfront project for six months just waiting on windows. Can you imagine paying all that money and not even having windows? 

But, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Right, being tired. Yeah. Just totally exhausted by everything. Even the small stuff just takes it all out of me.
Have you ever had a period in the past when you felt this way for at least two weeks—like you didn’t care about anything, felt hopeless, or lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

In the past? No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had stressful times, sure, but I've never felt like this before. Back when I was getting my Master's, that was stressful. I finished my degree back in '96, and the workload was just unbelievable. We used to practically live in the university library. There was this little diner right across the street, though, that made the most incredible cherry pie. Real sour cherries, not that overly sweet canned filling they use everywhere now. The owner, Sal, he had this massive, vintage espresso machine imported from Italy. All chrome, with a brass eagle sitting right on top of it. Just a beautiful piece of machinery. 

You really don't see craftsmanship like that anymore, do you? Everything now is just cheap plastic that breaks the second you look at it. I actually bought a new toaster just a couple of weeks ago, supposedly top of the line, and the lever just snapped right off in my hand on the third use. I tried calling their customer service, and I was on hold for forty-five minutes listening to this absolutely grating elevator jazz. It was just a synthesizer and a saxophone playing the same four bars over and over. I finally just hung up. I still have the broken toaster sitting on the counter because I don't even have the energy to throw it away. 

Anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling like this in the past. No, never. I've always been pretty steady until recently. I've never had a time where I just stopped caring about everything for weeks on end.
Have you ever had a period in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things for more than two weeks in the past?

I think... wait, didn't you just ask me that? I'm pretty sure you just asked me that. About feeling this way in the past? Yeah, I was just saying, no, I haven't. I've never felt like this before. It's just been recently that everything has gone downhill. 

Speaking of downhill, my sister was just telling me about her ski trip to Colorado. They go to Aspen every year. She said the snow this year was terrible, just complete ice on the lower runs. Her husband actually slipped and tweaked his knee walking out of the lodge. They had to spend half a day at the urgent care clinic. Those clinics are popping up everywhere now, aren't they? There used to be an old Blockbuster Video on the corner by my house, and now it's one of those urgent cares. I miss Blockbuster. Going in on a Friday night, hoping all the new releases weren't rented out yet. The smell of the popcorn they sold by the register. You just don't get that experience scrolling through Netflix. There are too many choices now, you know? You spend more time picking something to watch than actually watching it. I tried to watch a movie the other night, some action thing, but I just couldn't pay attention. I ended up turning it off after twenty minutes. 

But yeah, anyway, you did just ask me that, right? No, I haven't had a time like this in the past. Just this current stretch.
Have you had any periods in your life, even before this recent stretch, where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things for two weeks or more?

Doc, are you... are you feeling alright? Because I swear you just asked me that exact same thing. Like, literally two minutes ago. Are you testing my memory or something? 

My memory is fine. I mean, mostly fine. I did lose my keys the other day, but that's just because I set them down on top of the microwave instead of the hook by the door. I don't even know why I was near the microwave. I haven't cooked anything in weeks. The inside of it is probably disgusting. My old roommate in college, Dave, he never cleaned the microwave. He used to heat up these awful frozen burritos, the cheap ones that cost like fifty cents, and they would explode everywhere. Bean paste just caked on the ceiling of the microwave. Dave was a character, though. He ended up moving to Seattle to start a band right around the time grunge was getting huge. Played bass. He bought this vintage Fender Precision Bass at a pawn shop for practically nothing. You can't find deals like that anymore. Now everybody looks up what things are worth on eBay on their phones before they price them. The internet really ruined thrift shopping, didn't it? Used to be you could find real treasures, like first-edition books or... 

Wait. What was I saying? Oh, right. The question. No, seriously, doc. I've never felt like this in the past. This is the first time. I promise my answer hasn't changed since the last two times you asked.
Have you ever had a time in your life before this recent stretch when you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things for two weeks or more?

Okay, I... I really don't understand what's happening right now. Are you reading off a script or something? Because this is the fourth time you've asked me the exact same question. The fourth time. I'm sitting here telling you no, I haven't, and you just keep asking it. 

It reminds me of this telemarketer who kept calling my house last summer. Every single Tuesday at 6:15 PM, right when I used to sit down to eat dinner back when I actually had an appetite. They were trying to sell me some sort of extended warranty on a car I hadn't owned in ten years. A '98 Honda Civic. Great car, by the way. I drove that thing cross-country twice. The second time, I took the southern route through New Mexico and Arizona. The sunsets out there are just unbelievable, like the whole sky is on fire. You don't see colors like that on the East Coast. The air is different out there, too. Drier. I bought a turquoise ring at a roadside stand near Gallup. The guy who sold it to me said his grandfather made it. The silver work was incredible, really intricate stamping. I gave it to an ex-girlfriend, Sarah. I wonder what Sarah's doing now. She wanted to open a bakery, but flour prices went up, and... 

Look, I don't know how many different ways I can say it. No. I have never had a two-week period of feeling like this in the past. It's just happening now. Can we please move on to a different question?
